Hon. JACQUES BUREAU (Minister of Customs and Excise) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 225, to amend the Inland Revenue Act.
He said: The bill explains itself. The old clauses appear in the bill and the amendments are shown in italics. The first clause extends the interpretation of the word " chemist." When prosecutions 'were taken under the act it was often the case that the certificate of an assistant or junior chemist in the department, by whom the work was actually done, was refused by the court, and it became necessary to send our chemist down from the department to the court. The interpretation is extended to include any employee classified as junior chemist, assistant chemist or chemist in a laboratory in the Department of Customs and Excise or of any department of the government. The second clause makes the presentation of the certificate of the chemist prima facie evidence of his capacity to act as such. The third clause is to provide a penalty for those who deodorize denatured alcohol. Under part 10 of the Inland Revenue Act, only methylated alcohol was mentioned; we now add denatured alcohol.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

On section 99-Bank may sell assets to another bank.

The sections from 98 on to
103 I think are the sections under which mergers of banks are consummated. As I read the sections they are in Substantial conformity with the provisions of the act as it was revised in 1913. In other words there ha# been substantially no change. Now, in view of the fact that the banks have decreased from the number of twenty-four I think it was, to seventeen, does- not the minister think it advisable that some restricting clauses should be enacted which would prevent an undue centralization of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend would have difficulty in defining any way to accomplish that. I suppose he approaches this question from the point of view that a merger is necessarily a bad thing-
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-I am not able to concur in that view; I think there may be cases in which a merger is a very good thing. I have known cases in the past where a bank in fairly good position was on the down grade, and by being taken over by another bank it was saved; every good interest was promoted by the merger. There may be a similar case in the future. I am quite prepared to admit there may be need in the future of some mergers. I think as a rule they should be discouraged, but circumstances may arise which may render a merger necessary and proper. It has been suggested that a merger should only be made by a special act of parliament. I could not approve of that because the circumstances under which a merger mayr be deemed necessary may be very urgent, and to wait until parliament could convene might

be to destroy the possibility of the merger going through and to lead to serious trouble. I am not anxious to promote mergers unnecessarily, but I cannot conceive of any arrangement that could be made which would be better than that which we already have.

I observe that under the provisions of this bill the minister is empowered, if he considers it m the public interest, to give his consent to a merger. Well, during the last ten years one such application has been refused.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes?

And the remaining applications, I think some six or seven have been granted. Now, what I should like to have if possible is an enunciation of the principles upon which the merger should be allowed. What is meant by this vague term "in the public interest?" For instance, I understand that the Bank of Hamilton sought to merge with some other bank, but the application was refused on the ground that it was not "in the public interest."' Surely there should be some limitation to that very wide and vague term which means something to everybody and nothing to anybody in particular. It is like the phrase "adequate protection" which covers-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A multitude of sins.
Yes, it covers a multitude o' sins.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid that if my hon. friend were asked to suggest what conditions could be laid down he would have as much difficulty as I have in the matter. If it were a case of two large banks where the amalgamation involved a diminution, a material diminution, in competition it might be held there is no particularly good reason for the merger except some profit-making motive; there might be no public reason which would indicate its necessity. May I suggest to my hon. friend that all applications or suggestions for mergers do not come before the public in a formal way. Ministers of Finance are approached sometimes informally and are asked what they would think of a merger, and if they give an intimation that they do not think the merger is likely to be a useful thing that would probably be the end of it and there would be no formal application. As I said a moment ago I am not anxious to promote mergers 'but I quite realize, and I should expect, that if, after this bill passes, there should be applications for mergers, the minister, and the government acting co-ordinately with the minister.

Bank Act
will decide what the circumstances call for and what ought- to be refused. I really have difficulty in defining the matter more clearly than it is defined at present.
I wonder if the minister would care to state whether he has received information already regarding further mergers in Canada or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no proposal before me for any merger nor do I anticipate any coming at any early date.

I should like to ask the Minister of Finance whether in his opinion it is not in the interest of the public that there should be competition in banks as well as in all other organizations. The whole tendency is in the direction of mergers and I must say that I would look upon the movement with some degree of favour if we should see established a Bank of Canada. Such an institution would be a national bank, and more or less associated with smaller concerns. Something in that direction may be effected which would serve the interests of the public. Apparently, however, the tendency is to remove the competition that now exists in banking. Heretofore we have had a great many banks in this country serving the public, and when those desirous of getting accommodation cannot get service at one they may go to another. Still, the tendency is towards mergers, and if it continues there will not be very many banks left in the country. They will all be merged. The same thing has occurred in Great Britain. An enormous amount of merging has taken place there. I cannot say what the net result has been in Britain, but certainly there has been a great diminution in the number of banks, and the same thing is going on in many other countries. It is taking place in the United States. There have been mergers there, and especially mergers in connection with the railways. There have also been extensive mergers in Great Britain in connection with the railways. Where is this merging business going to end? We have got through a great war, and a great disturbance, and there have been many mergers and consolidations of this kind. Is it in the public interest that there should be these consolidations without having some explanation as to the underlying principles that ought to obtain in connection with mergers, especially of banks? While the minister says he has not heard anything of any likelihood of other mergers, there have been hints in the public press of other mergers coming, and coming in the city of Montreal. There may be other mergers under way which are directed from
Toronto, and the public certainly have some interest in knowing what ought to be the underlying principles. Those principles, if possible, ought to be embodied in the Bank Act with which we are now dealing. I do not see why there should not be a more explicit statement by the minister not only on behalf of himself and the department but on behalf of the public, as to what the government's attitude is toward this question of bank mergers. There is rather an attitude on the part of the public that they do not know exactly what is transpiring and the extent to which these mergers are going on. If up to date they have been all right, well and good, but I do not think such is the case.
There is another thing that has transpired in connection with the revision of the Bank Act this session and that is a direct refusal to permit the creation of smaller banks. Now, in the United States, which is a country very similar to ours, they have a provision in their banking laws which allows the establishment of smaller banks ,and these banks have been of great service to particular localities. In these localities the capitalists get together and establish a small bank for the encouragement of their particular district and the local industries, and I think they have done very substantial service to the country. But we have gone so far as to say that we do not want small banks, and we are allowing mergers to go on without any direct definition of the underlying policy or principle which should govern. We have heard from members from the Maritime provinces what has happened in that particular part of Canada in regard to the disappearance of banks. One of the strongest banks in the Dominion today came from one of the Maritime provinces. The administration, for example, of the Bank of Nova Scotia-and it is one of the best and most successful administrations in Canada, has been moved from the Maritime provinces. We have heard Maritime province members say that they look with a great deal of suspicion upon the disappearance of the local banks. I do not know how many strong Maritime province banks have disappeared during the last twenty years. The present Finance Minister, and previous Ministers of Finance, could doubtless justify this, but there is a suspicion in the minds of the public that there should not be this widespread merging of banks, and that there should not be this direct refusal to grant charters to small banks without a declaration of policy by parliament. If there is one good reason why the bank charters should only be granted for one year it is because all these questions are coming up.

Bank Act

Before we renew the charters for ten years we should settle the underlying principle on which mergers are to be allowed. We have the refusal of parliament at this time of revision to make any proper provision for the establishment of smaller banks. I am a great believer in the success of the small banks in the United States, notwithstanding the disasters which accompanied the administration of some small banks. I challenge the proposition that it would be a good thing for Canada to have more bank mergers. Competition is a good thing for trade, as has been said by many exponents of fiscal policies. I subscribe to that doctrine.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext:
How are you going to
compete?

Do not merge
them. Leave us what we have at least, or give us a good reason for having mergers.
I thought the hon. member believed in putting all our banks together?

I said that I
would not object to one large Bank of Canada, and not only one national bank, but one national reserve for all the banks, and a national system of currency, instead of the creation and widening of the principle of bank-note issue. We are now strengthening the right of the banks to issue their own notes, and they actually destroy the national notes as fast as they can get them; they put them out of business and substitute their own notes for the use of trade. We are now making the third revision of the Bank Act; we are revising it for ten years, notwithstanding the disclaimers that have been made; we are doing all this without a declaration of the underlying principle that ought to govern bank merge ns', without a real declaration in regard to what we ought to do in connection with the establishment of smaller banks, and we are declaring that this revision should be for ten years. If there is anything incumbent on parliament to-day it is that they should make a declaration in regard to these matters I have mentioned. We have a report presented by another committee which states, after careful study, that they are not prepared to say what ought to be done to widen the basis of credit, as it is called and this matter has been very carefully considered by the committee on Agricultural Conditions. In view of all these things, we ought to have a care at this time, and should not grant a renewal of the bank charters for ten years without an absolute
rMr. W. F, Maclean.]
declaration as to the underlying principles in the matters of mergers. Yet we are doing 'this at a time when there are hints of other mergers coming. I leave it to the members from the Maritime provinces to say whether they appreciate the disappearance of all the local banks which were doing business in their provinces. The world has been turned upside down by the war, and a new alignment is now under way, and I ask whether in view of the re-adjustment that is taking place, this new alignment should be on broad progressive lines, or in the direction of a conservative movement and the consolidation of capital in very few hands. If there is to be consolidation of capital, there will soon be a political movement in this and other countries for the distribution of the power of these immense consolidations of wealth, especially in connection with the banks, because the life of trade is banking, and the life of the farmer is banking. To-day the farmer is asking for an improved banking system, something he never had before and for which he has great need. One thing he asks for is the recognition of the smaller bank; yet the mergers are proceeding. The number of banks is now down to seventeen and later on the number will be down to twelve, then ten and perhaps nine. They will centre in Montreal; perhaps many of them will centre in Toronto. I maintain that it is not a good thing. In the Mother Country there are very powerful banks that have their influence outside of London, although the concentration is all in the direction of London, as the concentration of banking in the United States is in the direction of New York. In the States however they have something which we have not got, and they dealt with it in connection with their banking act. II refer to the creation of a national reserve bank system. I am not going into the detail of that, but I have read enough, have seen enough and studied enough to realize that the American national reserve bank system is the very thing we want in Canada.
Another thing we want is to have no issue except the national note for public business. If any public representative in the United States proposed that the banks should be allowed to destroy the national notes, what we call legal tenders-put them out of business and substitute their own issue in place of these notes-he would not get a hearing, and would not be re-elected. The tendency of the banking system in Canada is to put the national notes out of existence and substitute bank notes in their place. There is some reason for this, and I suspect that there is a great advantage to the banks in it. I main-

Bank Act
tain that there is some reason for the action of the banks when they take away the national notes and destroy them. They are putting the legal tenders out of business so fast that we will never see them. If the banks were very anxious to issue their notes for the purpose of serving the public, I would not have any great objection, but the whole tendency of the legislation this session has been to strengthen the banks, to increase their power, to destroy the national notes and the national reserve. I challenge the Minister of Finance, and I challenge his party and the banks of this country, to say why there should be two issues of notes in Canada, a bank note and a national note, and why the banks should be given an opportunity to put the national notes out of existence and substitute their own notes. Thait occurs very frequently.
Carried.

Is the hon. member for Halifax a merger man? Does he speak on behalf of the government? That is the issue? It is very easy to say "carried." Of course they can carry it, if that is the attitude of the party. I will give the government credit for trying to make things a little better for the country, but they have not succeeded.
Carried.

Somebody had better carry out the hon. member. Call in the carrier. I repeat that it is incumbent on the Minister of Finance to say whether he approves of mergers. So far he does not disapprove. But a public man in office, when his party has to assume the responsibility of carrying on the government, must deal with these questions as they arise. This question has arisen all over the country. Great scandals have been started in connection with one merger and we have not got the explanation of it yet. We cannot get it. We cannot get the witnesses before parliament. I am not going to name the merger, but hon. members know that one of the finest banks in the country disappeared not long ago. It was a splendid bank and had customers all over the country. The bank gave these customers a good service, and in the time of war these people were let out. Probably the bank that took over this bank took over the customers. But that is not a good merger. I hope before this discussion is over-and I am quite sure it is not over just yet, and that the section will not be carried in a moment-that we will have a definition of policy in regard to mergers and a further enlightenment as to
whether it is the policy of the government, now that we are revising the Bank Act for ten years, that there should be two sytems of bank reserves in this country, and two issues of notes, namely bank notes and national notes. We want a final declaration from -the government whether it would not be wise for this parliament under present circumstances to renew the Bank Act for another year or for two years, in order to allow parliament to take up all these questions of mergers and revisions, even the establishment of a national bank reserve system, and in connection with that a system of credit for the farmers. They want that, and they ought to unite in order to secure it. A national bank reserve system and a system of credit for the farmers ought to be part of this policy, or you will not afford relief where relief is asked for by the people of the West. For a moment I am going to leave the discussion, in order to give my hon. friends from the Maritime provinces an opportunity to say whether they are pleased with the mergers which have taken place, and to give some of the other members of the House an opportunity to say whether they think that for ten years longer we should prevent smaller banks from getting charters on a much smaller capitalization.

May I join my voice with those who have pointed out to the government the danger of permitting the continuation of mergers in this country? I have little to say as to the merits of concentration. I am not prepared to argue in favour of or against it at the present time; but the people are not at all satisfied that it is in the best interest of Canada that there should be a steady concentration of the money of the country in the hands of fewer and fewer men. The danger must be obvious to hon. gentlemen, when the control of capital is placed in the hands of private individuals who are not always actuated by the interest of the nation, but are more frequently actuated by their own gain. I think I may speak at any rate for my own constituents when I say that they are absolutely opposed, possibly for their own reasons, to the continuation of mergers in this country.

I do not think mergers can be stopped. I think the attitude of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is correct in this regard. At the same time, I do not think they should be encouraged for their own sake. Mergers are merely a passing phase of the economic system. I look forward to a time when they will be merged to the uttermost. Then, perhaps, we shall discover how to decentralize them in the interest of the people. I hope that before the next bank revision, we
Bank Act

shall have only one bank in Canada and one financial king upon the throne. Then, perhaps, we shall be in a position to do something better. Therefore, I hope the Minister of Finance will encourage as much as he possibly can the growing tendency to merge.

We are dealing with a clause relating to the purchase of the assets of a bank. People designate this as a " merger," and this word has been made unpopular, being often unfairly and improperly used. Hon. gentlemen talk about a merger as if it were a thing that could be prevented. The Minister of Finance has stated the government's policy, which is a sound one, namely, that it is not disposed to consent to the merging of banks each of which occupies a sound position merely for the sake of their being merged or for the sake of profit-making. But we must have in this act some provision whereby a bank may purchase the assets of another bank. Most mergers that have taken place in Canada were induced by the fact that the selling bank was in, or approaching, an insolvent position and the management were not disposed to carry on business further. It is in the interest of depositors and shareholders that there be a legal procedure to dispose of the assets of one bank to another. There could be only one other procedure for a bank approaching insolvency to adopt, and that would be to wind up; and it is preferable to give such a bank an opportunity of disposing of its assets under favourable terms to a bank already in existence. It would be a great mistake on the part of parliament to prevent that from being done. Further, I should like to point out that a bank cannot continue right up to a position of insolvency as an ordinary business concern might do. The slightest intimation of a weak position by a bank is the sign for withdrawal of deposits, and loss of credit, which mean the destruction of the bank. Personally, I have never been able to understand the criticism which has been directed against the merging of banks. Of course, we all believe that banks which occupy a strong solvent position should not be permitted to merge. When their solvency is threatened, when their business is on the decline and is bound to end some time, they should have the right under the law to merge with other banks.

speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 101-Agreement of sale to be submitted to selling shareholders at meeting.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Perhaps I might say a word or two anent the remarks of the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Maclean), as this clause has to do with the

carrying out of provisions of sale. My conception of the position is this. The attitude of the government against the merging of banks, while not obdurate and not absolutely antagonistic, should be just as close to that as there is any possibility of getting. I do not think it is right that there should go out word that as soon as a bank feels itself to be approaching insolvency, it can apply for and obtain consent to a merger. There might be conditions under which insolvency would be the best course. It is conceivable that a bank might bring itself into, at least, a seeming position of approaching insolvency in order that merging might result. But, even if it does not do that, the utmost resistance should generally be given against a merger until it is found to be absolutely impossible to do anything else, short of definite insolvency. I believe that was the attitude of the late Minister of Finance. I know representations were made that the descent to insolvency had commenced, where still resistance was given, and where finally there was no merger because there was no consent, and at the same time there was no insolvency I do not say that the directors, in the case I have in mind, were insincere in their representations that merging was absolutely necessary; but I know the resistance was successful in preventing a merger, and that the trend of events did not finally reach insolvency.
What I want to say is this. In my judgment, the fewer mergers we have the better, that is, of the banks that we have to-day My information is that in England they have fewer than we have in Canada, although they have a much larger population. Of course they have a somewhat different system. But the fewer we have the better, and the more adverse the attitude of the government and the Minister of Finance is towards mergers, the better for us. At the same time I quite admit that the hon. member who has just sat down is correct when he says that there comes a time when merging is the only way that can prevent very great hardship to shareholders or possible loss to depositors-in a word, to prevent the very things which the safeguards of the Bank Act are intended to prevent. But it should be the last resort, and the very last resort; and the bank should understand that such is the attitude of the government. It should understand that it is only as a rescue from inevitable insolvency that a merger can be assented to. I can think now of no other justifiable case.

I would add just a word or two after what the right hon.

Bank Act
gentleman has said. There should, I think, be some provision in the Bank Act to obviate the necessity for any banks approaching insolvency, which is the very thing complained about now. Probably the best safeguard against such a condition would lie in still more stringent regulations under the act. After some little observation of bank mergers in this country I have come to the conclusion that provision should be made in the act for an earlier examination into the condition of banks. Most of the mergers that have taken place ought to have been known either directly or indirectly to the Deputy Minister of Finance who, not by any public examination but by an examination of some sort, should have a way of finding out a year or two ahead the exact state of affairs in connection with the banks in order to prevent the things that lead to insolvency. As it is, we have no such provision. That is one reason why the Bank Act should be extended for only one year, so that at another session of parliament we might deal with this question, which is associated with the creation of a national reserve bank system and a system of credit for the convenience of farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With most of what my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) said regarding mergers I am heartily in accord. But he was perhaps too rigid in his statement that a merger should be allowed only when a bank could prove that it was on the eve of insolvency. That, I think, is too strong a statement to make. I have in mind the case of a merger which is not by any means recent having occurred some years ago, in connection with which the bank that was absorbed was entirely solvent when turned over to the other bank-it was not insolvent, nor indeed was it on the edge of insolvency. The directors, capable business men, reviewing the whole situation, saw however that the bank was on the decline, and that the day was coming when it could not be successful. They realized that if they persevered their shareholders would lose money, and in good time, before insolvency was absolutely in sight, they asked for a merger. I
4 p.m. do not know who was Minister of Finance at the time, I do not believe it was in my day; but they got permission and the merger took place. I am not dissenting from what my right hon. friend has said, but I would not suggest that a bank should prove that it was absolutely insolvent before being allowed a merger. The whole situation should be reviewed from the point of view of not desiring mergers; but
at the same time you do not want to sacrifice any existing institutions or destroy the property of shareholders if by allowing a merger in time you can safeguard that property.

I beg to move in amendment as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
That Bill 83 be not now read a third time but that it he referred back to Committee of the Whole with instructions that subsection 1 of section 5 of said bill be amended by substituting the word "twenty-four" for the word "thirty-three" in the fourth line thereof, and that subsection 2 of said section be amended by substituting the word "twenty-four" for the word "thirty-three" in the third line thereof.
I have a few remarks to make in that connection, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Who is the seconder?

The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey). I had intended some days ago speaking at some length on the situation that presents itself in connection with the revision of the Bank Act, and the granting of bank charters for a period of ten years; but I have concluded, after seeing the way things have been going during the last day or two, that it would be useless and inexpedient to speak of any of the matters I had in mind. I shall take another opportunity elsewhere to put myself on record.
Now, the substance of the amendment has already been debated in Committee of the
Bank Act

Whole and therefore there is no need at present to cover the ground again. But 1 should just like to say, Mr. Speaker, that in my judgment this matter, and the fundamental questions which are involved, have not been given any adequate consideration in the committee on Banking and Commerce. The economic situation in Canada is admittedly very serious at the present time, and that fact, together with all the circumstances which were outlined the other day in Committee of the Whole makes it highly desirable that the bank charters be not extended for the full period of ten years. Of course, if if is generally understood, as has been to some extent intimated, that the Bank Act is open for revision at any time, that may be satisfactory; but it has not, I think, been clearly and definitely so understood, and for (he purpose of clearing up what has been lest m a rather indeterminate condition I think this amendment is necessary.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there has been, perhaps, a good deal of feeling in the committee over some of the proceedings. I have personally felt that investigation, very necessary investigation, has been stifled. I have felt that at times very necessary discussion has been choked off, or that an attempt has been made to choke it off. I want to say further that the opposition to the course which has been taken by a number of the Progressive members has seemed to me to be entirely unworthy of those concerned. In that connection, and in conclusion-for I do not wish to speak at length I want to refer to an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Standard of 9th June, which was referred to yesterday, but not read, by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). I should like to submit this editorial to the judgment of the House as the sort of thing which we ought not to have in discussions on any public question. I think, Mr. Speaker, I am in order in reading this editorial or a part of it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member will find that according to paragraph 202 of Beauchesne's parliamentary rules and forms:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the House and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the House.
The hon. member will find that this is supported by Bourinot, page 336.

Mr. Speaker, referring to the
point of order, it seems to me that if you give the interpretation you seem inclined to give, it would cut out the reading of comment in any newspaper upon the proceedings of
fMr. Good.]
this House, or on any matter that is being dealt with here. I must confess I do not quite understand the rule. There is nothing in this editorial that reflects especially upon the integrity of any particular member so far as I know. It is simply comment such as we see continually in the public press upon the proceedings in this House.

Does it reflect
upon some hon. gentlemen who are in the House?
Not by name.
Does it insinuate something in regard to them? If not, perhaps it would be in order.

Perhaps the
article was written by a humourist and therefore should not be regarded as serious.
Do you rule me out of order in advance, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
I am simply directing
the attention of the hon. member to the pitfall. I do not know what the contents of the article are or the subject to which it refers. If the hon. member will give the gist of the editorial to the House, I might be in a better position to rule as to its admissibility.
I would be very glad, Sir, if you would give me permission to read the editorial and you could stop me if at any time you thought I should be stopped.
Go on.

The editorial, only part of which I shall read is as follows:
Time to digest the evidence-
This has reference to the position which the Progressives had taken in asking for more time to consider the evidence placed before the committee.
Time to digest the evidence is obviously a ruse, because one part of the evidence is indigestible save by progressive gastric juices and the other part formed a lump in their stomachs long ago. It is this lump, rejected by commonsense and good business, which gives rise to all their windy futilities in committee and in the House. The evidence has been chewed and rechewed by the paper money theorists time and again and any further chewing will not make it taste oi smell better.
The brethren from the West, who are bent on turning the banks inside out for their own benefit, are in no hurry to get home. They can make more money at Ottawa. It takes a lot of wheat to equal $4,000, almost aid of it net profit and no particulai toil involved.
I will omit a few sentences referring to two of the members of the committee by name. The editorial continues:
Of course there is no danger of the government being defeated by the Progressives. They are not

anxious for an election which would lead them into the wilderness, and no doubt the boldest held their breath when the government squeezed through with a majority of eight on the budget. But their pose is in peril and a display of firmness on the part of all the sound thinkers in the House will soon bring them to terms. We can also depend on the hot weather to take the starch out of their souls and the stiffening out of their necks.
Such being the case it looks as if Liberals and Conservatives could not do better than bury the hatchet for the nonce get together on a non-partisan measure-as the Bank Act is and press it to a vote. What the Progressives might think about it is comparatively unimportant, but it is important that this land of Canada should have a sound banking system.
I hope my reading of the editorial does not transgress the rules of the House. I just wanted to cite this as a sample of the sort of opposition which we sometimes have to meet, but I am not greatly worried over this kind of opposition.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: There is a misunderstanding. I thought it proper to let the hon. member read the gist or the substance of the editorial to the House. As a matter of fact it is out of order, because it has no bearing on the present amendment moved by the hon. member, but I must say that what the hon. member has just read might be the subject of a question of privilege, because it contains a reference to some hon. members of the House, but it has no bearing on the present amendment.

I am not as familiar with the rules of the House as I would like to be, and if this particular matter should have been referred to under another heading, I must, of course, apologize for bringing it up in this connection. I submit, however, that it has a very distinct relevance to the question under discussion, because the amendment is for a reference of the bill back to the Committee of the Whole with instructions as to the amending of clause 5, and the editorial which I have read seems to me to have specific reference to the amendment which I have just moved in that it refers to our claim made hitherto, as to the need for further time for considering this question. However, I do not think there is any need at the present time to prolong the discussion on this matter. It received a good deal of ventilation in the Committee of the Whole the other day, and I presume every one here has made up his mind in regard to it; so that I shall say no more.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Before the question is
put, I want to put, in a word or two, the reasons for my vote. I cannot review to any advantage what the hon. mover of the
Bank Act
amendment has said. I was not a member of the committee and I do not know personally of its conduct. He charges that there was a stifling of discussion and blocking in that committee. I hope the allegation is not correct; I would be sorry to think it was correct as against the Chairman, or indeed against the majority of those present. But, remembering that it was not long since I wa3 charged with being a stifler and a blocker myself, I want to be charitable to those who, the assailants of that day, are now charged with the same offence. I am very glad, Mr. Speaker, that you did not enforce the rule by prohibiting the reading of the editorial, because I remember that that rule has been always more honoured in the breach than in the observance. In fact, I can recall the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding), at a very recent date, quoting the Ottawa correspondent of the Montreal Gazette in support of the theory that he made a very excellent budget speech; consequently I am glad it was not enforced on this occasion against the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good). As to the allegations in the editorial about Liberals and Conservatives getting together in order to defeat the Progressives, I have to say that I am unmoved. I purpose to take my position on this clause on the same principles I endeavour to apply with regard to all public questions, that is on my judgment of its merits. From that judgment I do not intend to be swayed either by the adhesion of a proselyte or by the antagonism of a foe. The question is whether the act should be extended for ten years or only for one. To commence with, unless there is strong reason to the contrary, it is, of course, presumable that it is better to extend it for ten years. If one-year extensions would serve the purpose of the country generally speaking as well as ten, it is presumable that they would have been adopted long ago.
It does not take any reflection to convince one that one-year extensions would not be favourable to the conduct of public business. I do not know how public business could be carried on if there was a sword of suspension hanging over the whole financial fabric of the nation that might be brought down every twelve months-
May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes.
Does the hon. member understand the amendment to mean that the charters shall be granted year by year?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No, I was merely saying that it was presumable that, unless there were strong reasons to the contrary, it was better
Bank Act

for public business that the extension be for ten years, and I fortify that by saying that otherwise it would have been the practice of this parliament to grant yearly extensions. The reason yearly extensions are not granted is because, under yearly extensions, anything in the nature of stability and continuity of business would be impossible.
But hon. members say, here is a special case, and there should now be only a yearly extension for this one time. I listened to arguments the other day in support of that contention. As I grasped them-and I may not have succeeded in getting them all, or perhaps in getting any of them right, although I listened to four or five speeches-they may be summarized as follows: First, that there is' in contemplation on the part of those who favour the amendment and, perhaps, generally, certain legislation looking to the establishment of rural credit banks or some other system that will take care of the demand for loans now not capable of being met by either the loan companies or the banks, and that if when it comes to the point of considering such legislation, we are confronted with a definite ten-year extension of the Bank Act, we shall not be in favourable circumstances to establish this competing institution. I have stated this in the best terms I can. Stated in that way, I do not see any force to it. Wherein will conditions be unfavourable for its establishment, conditions that would be favourable if there was an extension for only one year? One hon. member suggested that the funds would be in the financial control, as he expressed it, in the hands, of the banks. Any funds in the banks at that time are withdrawable at once or on very short notice, and if depositors, the owners of the funds, wish to transfer them to the new institution, I do not know what would stand in their way, nor do I know of anything that would stand in their way that would not likewise stand in their way if a yearly instead of ten year extension were given. What is meant by "financial control?" There has to be somebody in control of our banks, but there would be just the same control on a one-year as on a ten-year extension. I do not know whether I grasp the argument as sought to be presented. Perhaps I do not. It really does not strike me as being capable of expression in a plausible way at all.
But it was said, if at that time the heads of our banking institutions find themselves secure behind a ten-year extension, they will not be disposed to come to parliament and to give the assistance that might be expected of, them towards the working out of legislation for a rural credit system. This is more plausible, but I do not think it has force.

For myself, I do not like to think the establishment of a rural credit system would at any time depend upon the assistance it would get from those who are now responsible for our chartered banks. I think it will have to get its inspiration and its support mainly from other sources. I do not think it will be wanting in either inspiration or support because the established institutions do not look with favour on it. It seems to me that we shall be just as well equipped a year from now as we are to-day or a year from now as we would be in ten, though there is an extension for ten years. I think the management of the banks will give us what is their opinion at that time, nowith-standing the fact that they have a ten-year extension; but as managers of going institutions that have been established for a long time, their opinions will naturally, and conscientiously, be formed in the atmosphere of those institutions, and they will not be favourable to something which is in the nature of an intrusion.

In the case of the
establishment of a rural credit system, if the banks were unfavourable, where would the right hon. member suggest that we could get the money from?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not think a rural
credit system will ever be established on the basis of a forced extraction of money from the banks. It could not be established on that basis. Consequently, it will not matter at all whether the answer to the hon. member's question is, "yea" or, "nay." In a word, so far as money is going to be necessary for rural credits, the will of the owner of the money will have to be brought into a favourable state of mind to apply the money to that purpose and towards that institution.

Would the right hon. gentleman be prepared to admit that if the bank charters had not been extended for ten years, the bankers would be more likely to take a co-operative attitude with a rural credit system, in the way of supplying the requirements?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not think that will make a bit of difference to them. I do not expect they will be in a co-operative attitude at any time; I do not think the rural credit system depends upon that at all, it depends upon the soundness of the priciples on which it is worked out. One of those principles can never be the compulsory taking of money from banks or from any individuals whatsoever.

Who suggested the compulsory taking of any money from the banks?

Bank Act

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). He wanted to know where we were going to get the money from if the banks' charter were extended. The question has no meaning unless it is intended to get the money by compulsorily taking it from the banks.
I do not think that inference is fair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not know, then, what the intention was.

In the United States they have made the national reserve bank system, every bank, the Comptroller of the Currency and the Secretary of the Treasury-as a matter of fact, the whole banking system of the United States-a part of the rural credit system. It might be necessary to do so. I shall have something to say later, but I am just intervening to say that, so to speak, this is a part of the national banking system of the United States to-day.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that the national banking system was under some compulsion to the reserve banks. Undoubtedly. I do not know that it was under any compulsion to the rural credit system.
Yes, it is.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not think it is. I do not pretend to have very recent knowledge at hand, but at one time I went pretty thoroughly into the question. I do not think the rural credit system of the United States rests in any degree at all upon compulsory contribution of banks. If that could be established, there would be some force in the observations of some hon. gentlemen who have argued in favour of the amendments.
I fancy I have reviewed all that has been argued in favour of the amendment, save one observation which had to do with another sphere of the discussion altogether. It was stated that there -was this overdue investigation into the conduct of certain officers of one of our banks, the Merchants Bank, and that the extension should be temporary as a lever to make certain investigations. Agair I do not see the force of the lever. I do not see how a temporary or a ten-year extension has anything to do with bringing about, oi deferring, or squelching, an investigation. It does not appear to me that the objects sought to be gained, though they may be valuable, will be in the least prejudiced by the ten-year extension. Very well, unless there is a forcible reason, one is not justified in voting for a one-year extension. This has been
a pretty barren session, but I do not want to contribute to make it more barren than it appears likely to result now. If we have a one-year extension, we have to go over all the work that this committee went through this year. We shall likely have plenty to do next session without that. From what I have learned of the committee, I believe it certainly went very laboriously and, I am disposed to think, pretty thoroughly about its task. Do we want to face next session with the whole thing to be reviewed once more? If we do, it means just that much less attention next session to other business that is going to demand all the time of hon. members of this House. Besides, it is undoubtedly correct-and I would not do justice to myself if I did not say it-that anything in the nature of a twelve-months' extension at this period in our commercial history, when a strain is being felt everywhere, would result in an instability and a sense of insecurity, the reflex action of which would come right back upon the borrowing public of the country. Of that there seems to my mind to be no reasonable or logical doubt whatever. Consequently, I feel like voting against the amendment and in support of the clause as it stands.
Mr Speaker-
Have you anything new to say?

Yes, I assure the hon. member that I shall have something new to say before I am through. I had no intention of speaking on this occasion, but the remarks of the leader of the Opposition necessitate my rising. I regret that the right hon. gentleman was not a member of the committee on Banking and Commerce so that he could have seen just how the inquiry was conducted. I understood him to say that he thought we had gone into the matter thoroughly. Well, I may observe that we went into the matter as thoroughly as we were allowed to do. In the subcommittee of the committee on Banking and Commerce, which was charged with the duty of calling witnesses, an application was made at its first meeting, I think, to have Mr. Macarow of the Merchants Bank called to give evidence. That application was refused.

If the hon. member will permit me, I might inform the House that Mr. Macarow's name was not suggested at the first meeting. It was suggested subse-
Bank Act

quently and the committee decided to postpone the decision as to whether or not he should be called. The subcommittee did not meet again and the matter was dealt witn by the general committee.

In that case I am corrected by the hon. member. At any rate, the fa:t remains that the application to have this gentleman called was refused. That subcommittee also recommended that Mr. Baker be requested to give evidence before the committee, but Mr. Baker did not appear. Later on it was moved in the committee by one hon. member that this gentleman should be [DOT]summoned to give evidence; the committee voted that proposition down and we were not allowed to have the benefit of Mr. Baker's evidence. Sir John Aird and Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor both appeared before the committee and if I remember correctly on both occasions the chairman of the committee gave the assurance that these gentlemen would be back again The questioning of these witnesses was largely in regard to the investigation, in connection with the motion of the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine), into the basis of credit, and not very generally in regard to the Bank Act as it was presented to us. Later on in the committee I moved that these gentlemen be recalled with the particular purpose in view of securing some details of the cost of running their western branches, in view of the statement they had made that they could not earn7 on under a maximum rate of interest of 7 per cent. The principal question, it seems to me, has not been touched upon, and that is the very serious situation that exists to-daj7 in the banking business of Canada, and the utter inadequacy of the present Bank Act to deal with that situation. When it is urged that we should have short-term credits or that we should have only those kinds of credits that can be readily cared for by the banks, I can see that there may be very considerable danger of invading the province which the banks have claimed for themselves. By this act we are granting certain privileges to these institutions which, if we later attempt to introduce something like a rural credit scheme, may be found to be seriously infringed upon. That is what I had in view when I asked the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) where the money would come from if it should be found wise to introduce some such scheme in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, while I am in sympathy with the motion, I am an absolute believer in the supremacy of parliament in the matter of legislation; in the right of parliament to change the Bank Act or any other act at any time. I may add that we shall be forced to change the Bank Act, in my opinion, at a very much earlier day than ten years from now, having regard to the circumstances that are developing. So I am here to vote for this limitation in order to allow parliament to deal with the question, but I point out that we have the right to reopen it at any time- the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has stated it; the chairman of the Banking
committee (Mr. Maclean, Halifax), has stated it. Parliament has the supreme right to reopen any question, notwithstanding any limitation that may be imposed at this time. The Criminal Code can be amended at any time; so can the Railway Act. But privilege is coming forward and saying that there shall be an amendment to the Bank Act only once in ten years. Well, that is not in the British North America Act; that has not formed part of the parliamentary policy of free people, of people subject to the democratic and the progressive rule that we have here and that they have in the Mother Country. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), and the hon. members of the committee generally will, I am sure, agree with me in this view. We are giving now the greatest privilege that can be given in connection with our financial institutions, and while I agree that there should be stability I object to its being stated here to-day that a privilege should be created for the banks of this country for a period of ten years and should not be interfered with during that time.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to prolong unduly this very interesting series, but I have an amendment which introduces a very important subject. 1 may say that, in substance, it is the same amendment that I attempted to bring into the House on a previous occasion, and it deals with the matter of the Merchants Bank. Since the Bank Act was last revised, there has occurred a very vicious . and cynical attack upon the principles of rectitude and integrity that are supposed to lie at the very root of our Canadian civilization, and the flagrancv of that act seems to be exceeded only by the complacency with which some hon. members in this House are prepared to see it sink into oblivion. I will content myself with reading the amendment. Some of us on this side of the House think the responsibility for pushing through this Bank Act without an inquiry into the Merchants Bank case ought not to rest upon any committee, but ought to be laid where it belongs, at the door of the House as a whole. I therefore beg to move:
That all the words after "that" be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
"Whereas the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce decided by resolution not to hear evidence dealing with the collapse of the Merchants Bank, and its subsequent amalgamation or absorption with the Bank of Montreal;
And whereas it is in the public interest that the conditions which led to or were connected with said collapse should be made public, in order that any weaknesses or deficiencies in the existing Bank Act may be remedied, and the interests of depositors, shareholders, and the general public may be safeguarded:
And whereas it is in the public interest that the facts surrounding the said amalgamation or absorption should be made public, in order that appropriate action may be taken by parliament, to prevent improper financial combinations and undue centralization in the control of financial credit in Canada.
Therefore be it resolved that Bill No. 83 be not now read a third time, but that the said bill be referred back to the standing committee on Banking and Com-

merce, with instructions that it have power to call and hear evidence concerning the said collapse and the said amalgamation or absorption, and that it have power to make such recommendations in the premises as may be deemed advisable."

This bank was organized in 1864 and at the time of its collapse had 389 branches functioning in all parts of Canada, except the province of Prince Edward Island and the Yukon. It stood third among the chartered banks of Canada in respect of the number of branches. It made a special effort to minister to the agricultural requirements of the country, for we find that of its total number of branches 147 were located in the three western provinces; and in the province of Alberta it led all other chartered banks with a total of 75 branches. In this connection I would observe-because I do not want to be misunderstood-that the losses that caused the collapse of the Merchants Bank did not arise in western Canada; they clearly arose in eastern Canada.
The success of this bank is not measured by the number of its branches, because I find that in the value of its assets, according to the last statement submitted, it stood fifth among the chartered banks of Canada, with assets totalling $182,000,000. Its liabilities to the public were $161,000,000, of which amount the responsibility to its depositors totalled the not inconsiderable sum of $130,000,000. It had an unimpaired reserve, according to the figures submitted, of $9,500,000. In addition to that I might point out that this bank, for a number of years paid a dividend of 12 per cent to its shareholders, and its shares immediately prior to the collapse brought on the market $160 each. So that generally speaking it may be said, so far as the public was concerned, that the Merchants Bank of Canada has an apparent financial stability, and merited in no limited degree the public confidence and esteem which it enjoyed. Very suddenly the scene is changed. Early in December, of 1921, the president of the bank, Sir Montagu Allan, issued a statement in which he pointed out two or three rather important facts. He pointed out that there had been large losses suffered by the bank which losses had been undisclosed to the directors, and that as a result there had been a very serious impairment in the reserve. He also stated that one Mr. Mackenzie, who, I believe, was general manager of the Royal Trust Company-an institution which has been called in this House the backdoor of the Bank of Montreal-had been employed for the purpose of making an audit some months before and had disclosed the particular facts to which I have alluded. Finally, the president stated that an absorption into the Bank of Montreal had been arranged, and among other details he mentioned that two Merchants Bank shares, would be exchanged for one Bank of Montreal share and the sum of $10.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was detailing the statement made by the president of the Merchants Bank in the preliminary announcement he gave to the public in December, 1921. Needless to say, an announcement of that character and made under such circumstances created considerable consternation. By the shareholders it was received with feelings of dismay, because the proposed arrangement made with the Bank of Montreal represented a loss to them alone of approximately five and a quarter millions of dollars. In addition to that it represented a very severe loss to the employees of the Merchants Bank, because the pension fund to which they were entitled and which formed part of the inducement held out to them in connection with the services they were rendering, was represented in the form of shares of that bank. After a short delay the Finance Minister of the day gave his preliminary consent to the absorption, pointing out that the only alternative was insolvency and loss. As required by law the shareholders of the Merchants Bank subsequently met, I believe, on the 8th of February for the purpose of approving the arrangement which had been entered into with the Bank of Montreal.
According to the published reports, the president of the Merchants Bank, Sir Montagu Allan, gave some further facts at that meeting. He pointed out that a firm of stockbrokers in Montreal which had become insolvent owed the Merchants Bank something like $4,500,000; that the debt of this firm to the bank had increased from $579,000 in April, 1916, to over $4,500,000 at the time of the firm's collapse in July, 1920, and that owing to the appalling inadequacy of the security and collaterals held by the bank, the bank suffered a loss of approximately $4,000,000. The president further pointed out that a debt owing by an organization called Exclusive Ladies' Wear and two or three allied organizations amounted in December, 1916, to almost a quarter of a million dollars, but that it had increased until in 1920 it stood at a total of $1,300,000. As a result of these two transactions alone the bank lost considerably

Bank Act

over $5,000,000. The president himself described the transactions to which I have referred as adventurous banking, but it seems to me that the amazing insufficiency of the security which was held by the bank justified the use of a very much harsher term.
By reason of these and other minor transactions the president pointed out that the bank's reserve had been reduced to meet these losses from nine and a half million dollars to one and a half million dollars. The shareholders at the meeting in question approved of the agreement and voted down a resolution that an inquiry should be conducted by the Dominion government to ascertain the responsibility for the situation which existed. It is only fair to say that the resolution was voted down not by the shareholders in person, but by reason of proxies held by the officers of the bank.
In addition to these facts mentioned by the president at that meeting to which I have referred, there were one or two other interesting facts disclosed. It was made apparent there that the Bankers' Trust Company, a subsidiary of the Merchants Bank, had in the months of October, November and December preceding the collapse sold some seven hundred sharjs of the bank stock at the market price then prevailing. The Bankers' Trust Company had in these sales secured the prices which prevailed for the Merchants Bank stock prior to the decrease caused by the announcement of the collapse.
Another fact disclosed was that on December 9th a committee had been appointed by the bank directors, consisting of the president, the vice-president, and I think Mr. Ballan-tyne, for the purpose of entering into negotiations with any bank or banks which might have a proposition to offer in connection with the sale of the Merchants Bank's assets. That, mark you, was on December 9th. It also transpired at the same meeting that on December 8th, the day preceding the Merchants Bank directors had received the offer from the Bank of Montreal which was at that meeting approved and which subsequently was carried into effect. In due course the Bank of Montreal shareholders met and ap proved of the arrangement. One of the officers of that bank in giving his reasons for the approval suggested that the acquisition of the Merchants Bank would give to the Bank of Montreal a number of branches in places where formerly they had very little representaton.

May I, in that connection, read a statement made by Sir Edmund Walker to substantiate the view which I hold. This question was asked Sir Edrthrad Walker when he gave evidence before the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce:
Q. Do you agree with Sir John Aird, if I understood him correctly, that the merger should not have been allowed to take place between the Bank of Montreal and the- Merchants?
A. Of course that depends on what the real condition of the Merchants Bank was, and none of us have been allowed to see that. Sir John makes that statement upon the basis of a statement made at the time by those who seemed to be in authority, that the Merchants Bank still had a surplus of about $1,000,000 odd; and his opinion was, that if it had its original capital and a surplus of $1,000,000 then it should not have been allowed to fail.
He was asked:
Q. Would you concur with him in that view'?
A. I would. I would also recall the fact that the Merchants had once a capital of $9,000,000 and lost its entire reserve and $3,000,000 of its capital and began business again and succeeded. It altogether depends on what the real conditions with the Merchant's Bank were, and none of us know that.

A. I don't know.
Q. Why should we not know?
A. Well, I don't know that either. I may tell you that my feelings are with the feelings of the most of the people in Canada on that subject.
He was further asked:

A. No, we have never been allowed to know anything more.
Q. Don't you think it is desirable that the public should know the whole history of this particular transaction?
A. Well as a fellow banker with the Bank of Montreal and the rest, I hesitate to answer that, but I may say we were all of us very indignant that we have not known more.
And then, I think, he suggested in another place that it certainly would be desirable to have the full facts disclosed. And so, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that if Sir Edmund Walker and Sir John Aird, bankers of the highest eminence in this country, are not apprized of
