I may say, Mr. Speaker, that an effort was made in the Banking committee to have these facts disclosed, to have them thoroughly investigated. A motion was made for the purpose of calling certain witflesses who would know about these facts. That resolution, I regret to say, was voted down by the committee. In order to secure a discussion on this matter in the House, in order to get the direction of the House on this important question, a further motion was moved that the committee should report to the House the action it had taken on the previous resolution and, strange to relate, the majority of the committee refused to even present to the House the action which they had taken in that connection. Consequently by the action of the committee this House has bes 1 effectively barred from discussing the Merchants Bank matter, or the advisability of inquiring into it, until the present moment. May I say that at that time it was urged by the Minister of Finance that it was not desirable that Sir Montagu Allan and Mr. Macarow, should be tried a second time. Nobody suggested they should be tried a second time. Nobody desires they should be tried a second time. The fact that a man has been tried on a particular criminal charge does not justify this House in refusing to call witnesses to ascertain material facts in the matter, and, as I have already pointed out, these defendants would not in the slightest degree be placed in jeopardy again; they would be entitled to claim and would secure from the committee the usual right which anyone secures under such circumstances, that any evidence given by them could not, under any circumstances, be used against them in any subsequent proceedings-unless, of course, it was necessary to use it in the event of perjury having been committed.
The point is this, Mr. Speaker: Under the existing Bank Act, the Merchants Bank collapse took place. Under the existing Bank Act the merger with the Bank of Montreal took place. Surely it is not unreasonable to suggest that the facts and circumstances in connection with these two matters should be investigated thoroughly, if you want to adequately provide, as far as it is humanly pos-

Bank Act
sible, against similar disasters in the future. I think that is not an unreasonable position. On the other hand, I think it is entirely businesslike, and is what is expected of this parliament. In addition to that fact there can be no question that under the provisions of the Bank Act there is an increasing concentration of the credit power of this country in the hands of a decreasing number of people, and despite that fact, despite the absorption under these circumstances by the Bank of Montreal, we leave these particular sections of the act dealing with mergers in exactly the same form they were ten years ago. We have no improvements to offer, because, of course, we have not the facts upon which to base any improvement.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that we. as the trustees of the people's interest, cannot stand by indifferently and see the interest of shareholders, of depositors and even the public credit of this country imperilled. It is, if I understand it correctly, our duty and oui obligation, as far as we possibly can, to prevent, by legislation, like disaster in the future Suppose, for instance, that the Bank of Montreal had not come to the rescue of the Merchants Bank, is there any one in this House who can set a limit to the disaster which would have followed? Depositors, shareholders and creditors would, alike have gone down in a crash of insolvency, and the credit of this country would have been seriously injured for years to come. Now, surely we are not going to allow, if it is possible to prevent, a creature of this parliament imperilling and placing in jeopardy the intersets of the people and the country, and rely only upon either the ambition or the generosity of a competing institution for safety. That is the suggestion which I make. For forty years in this country manufacturing industry has leaned upon parliament. Do we propose now that parliament, in order to preserve the interests of its people and preserve its own credit, shall rely upon a creature of its own creation? It seems to me that the position which we take in this matter, as designated in this resolution, is absolutely sound. The facts should be fully disclosed. In the light of these facts it may be that such legislation may be proposed as will prevent a similar unfortunate fiasco and disaster in the future.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with all the respect I desire to accord to my good friend from Calgary West (Mr. Shaw), and to those who agree with him in this matter, I am going to submit to the House that of the many reasons that are given for the delay of this Bank
Act, the weakest of all is this story about the investigation of the Merchants Bank. . There is no greater delusion in the whole discussion than the allegation that the public are demanding an investigation into the Merchants Bank. There is no foundation for it in the world. There is no indication that any person who has a penny of interest in the Merchants Bank is asking for investigation, and there is no shadow of connection between the Bank Act and the Merchants Bank investigation. If you had all the investigation in the world, and produced all the results you could produce, you would not bring forth any reason against the Bank Act. Who are complaining? The failure, as you call it, of the Merchants Bank, did not involve a penny of loss to any person in the country, except the shareholders. The hon. member speaks of depositors. The depositors have not suffered any. They are not grumbling. The note holders did not suffer. They are not grumbling. The shareholders did suffer, and they are not grumbling. There is not an application from any shareholder to interfere in this matter at all. I think they have the good sense to see that by letting the matter alone they get the best results. At all events, though at the time there was some irritation, the fact to-day is that the demand for investigation into the Merchants Bank comes from people who, at all events, whatever their good motives may be, have not a penny of interest in it. There is no public interest to-day which demands an investigation into the Merchants Bank. The people who have interest in the matter have their remedy, and apparently they are content. If any shareholder of the Merchants Bank-and he is the only one affected-feels that he has been unjustly treated through the action of the directors or the neglect of the directors, or that he has suffered a penny of loss, he has his remedy in the courts of the country and knows it.
What is the use of talking about shareholders being treated badly? The institution was an unfortunate one. Why constantly talk about the mystery of the Merchants Bank? There is no mystery in the world about it. There is no transaction in public affairs better understood than the Merchants Bank affair-no mystery about it. One hon. member thought it was an extraordinary thing that the Bank Act allowed $10,000,000 to slip away between the bars. There is no mystery about a ten cent piece of the money of the Merchants Bank. They got into trouble by reckless mismanagement. They lent money without security. They lent money to a brokerage firm in Montreal and they should not have done it. They lent money to many
Bank Act

people, and the evidence and the whole record . are there. There is no mystery about it. Everybody knows the cause of the disaster, and in a certain sense it was a disaster. Hon. members will find out that the people who are really interested are not grumbling. The world is full of idle curiosity. I suppose some persons would like to know more about it, but no public interest would be served by further investigation. Every weakness in the Bank Act that was disclosed by the Merchants Bank failure has been met and covered in the bill now before the committee. Accusations were made. The only charge that could be brought against the Merchants Bank by the government was that they had falsified the return. That accusation was made. It was sustained, so far as the department is concerned. Proceedings were taken. The trial took place. These two gentlemen who were accused were acquitted. Hon. members may have their opinions as to whether they should have been acquitted or not. What odds about that? They have been tried by the courts of the country. My hon. friends have an idea that either the Minister of Justice or the Finance Minister should have gone down to Montreal, seized Sir Montagu Allan by the scruff of the neck and taken him to prison. Those men were tried by the courts of the country and acquitted.
What more could be done? There is no mystery about it. Every penny that was lost is known to the public. The shareholders know all about it, and so far as I know they are all content-not content in the broadest sense because they have lost money, but I think they have come to the conclusion that, if things had not proceeded in that particular way, they would have lost more. I submit there is no connection between an investigation into the Merchants Bank and the bill we now have before the House. There is no reason in the world why we should delay this bill for one minute for the sake of an investigation into the Merchants Bank which could not accomplish anything and which nobody who is really interested in the bank's affairs seems to want.

The Minister of Finance has made a very brave attempt to defend a very bad case. I had a letter the other day from a shareholder of the Merchants Bank, whom I do not know at all and never did know, who happens to be in the United States now. I am sorry I did nos bring the letter down here. I have it upstairs.
Go and get it.

A very irate letter indeed,
endorsing, if I remember the terms of it,

most emphatically the stand that we have taken in this connection. I simply offer that as a bit of evidence in refutation of the statement made by the Minister of Finance that there has been no demand from the shareholders for an investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend aware that if that shareholder has a grievance he has his remedy in the civil courts and does not need to come here at all?

It is a small fact to which
I refer, not for the purpose of attaching any great importance to it, because I do not know that the shareholders are primarily interested. I think the people of Canada are interested in this matter far more than the shareholders. The Minister of Finance says that there is no mystery about this matter. All I have to say is that if we had an investigation, we would be in a position to know. We have had no investigation into the material facts, into the really essential and vital facts of the case, I mean the facts that are important to the Canadian people. We have had an investigation into the facts of the case in so far as they relate to the specific charges that were made against the two gentlemen mentioned. But those are not the facts in which I am interested. I am not a shareholder of the Merchants Bank; but I am responsible for some of the business and the institutions of this country, and so far as my share of the responsibility goes on behalf of the Canadian people, I think this is a matter that ought to be sifted to the very bottom.

Why did my
hon. friend not in the month of February make a motion in parliament to grant an inquiry? Or, if he forgot this in February, why did he not make it in March? If it escaped his attention in March, why did he not do it in April? Then he had all the month of May in which to do it.

I did what I could on the
committee to have investigation made.

The hon.
member should have done it in parliament.

The facts of the case have
already been presented by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw). If the demand which was made in the committee for the summoning of those two or three gentlemen who were in a position to give the facts, had been acceded to, I should have been satisfied. Why did I not make a demand in parliament earlier? Well, perhaps I thought the committee was the right place, at all

Bank Act
events the first place where the demand should be made. The committee was instructed to revise the Bank Act, and as has been shown, this particular inquiry is entirely relevant to the revision of the Bank Act. We did what we could; I did what I could on the committee, to secure the presence of these men in order that we might get information from them. As has been already stated, we failed. On two occasions we were voted down. The committee even voted down a request that the action of the committee taken at an earlier time should be reported to the House, so that the House might then take action if it thought fit to get those men here. That was voted down also. The matter was pressed twice before the committee, and on both occasions the lid was kept screwed down. Sometimes one gets suspicious by reason of the very effort that has been made to prevent an investigation. I do not know whether there is anything wrong or not; but when an effort is made to stifle investigation, I cannot help being suspicious.
There is another aspect of this situation that I would like to mention to-night before the vote is called. I refer to the question of mergers, to the question ov financial concentration. I have in my hand a book by a man who is now, I think, one of the judges of the Supreme Court of the United States. I refer to Louis D. Brandeis. His book is entitled "Other People's Money and How the Bankers Use It." I have referred to this book on one or two occasions in the committee, and I would like to refer to it again here.

Who is
Mr. Brandeis?

He is one of the judges of the Supreme Court of the United States, and I gather from reading the book that he had to do with a number of investigations in the United States some years ago in regard to "big business," if I may use that expression. I may say that the book is descriptive of conditions in the United States, and I think it has a direct bearing upon the situation in Canada and upon the case which we have now under consideration. I should like to quote a paragraph which the writer quotes from a statement made by ex-President Woodrow Wilson in 1911. I read:
The great monopoly in this country is the money monopoly. So long as that exists, our oid variety and freedom and individual energy of development are out of the question. A great industrial nation is controlled hy its system of credit. Our system of credit is concentrated. The growth of the nation, therefore, and all our activities are in the hands of a few men, who, even if their actions be honest and intended for the public interest, are necessarily concentratd upon
the great undertakings in which their own money is involved and who, necessarily, by every reason of their own limitations, chill and cheek and destroy genuine economio freedon. This is the greatest question of all; and to this, statesmen must address themselves with an earnest determination to serve the long future and the true liberties of men.
That was written by ex-President Woodrow Wilson in 1911. Further on in the first chapter of this book, the writer refers to the way in which the financial oligarchy in the United States extended their operations and gained control of the security makers on the one hand and the security buyers on the other-the large insurance companies and so on. I will read just one or two other extracts from this book. Here is a paragraph under the sub-heading, "Why the banks became investment bankers":
These large profits from promotions-
He is referring to the operations of J. P. Morgan and Co.
-underwritings and security purchases led to a revolutionary change in the conduct of our leading banking institutions. It was obvious that control by the investment bankers of the deposits in banks and trust companies was an essential element in their securing these huge profits. And the bank officers naturally asked, "Why then should not the banks and trust companies share in so profitable a field? Why should not they themselves become investment bankers too, with all the new functions incident to 'big business'?" To do so would involve a departure from the legitimate sphere of the banking business, which is the making of temporary loans to business concerns. But the temptation was irresistible. The invasion of the investment banker into the banks' field of operation was followed by a counter invasion by the banks into the realm of the investment banker.
Then he goes on to mention a number of United States banks which did this very thing.
The next chapter is entitled:
How the combiners combine.
Further on chapter 3 is devoted to interlocking directorates, the question which was discussed in such an illuminating way last year in this House by the hon member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). I want to read one or two paragraphs from this chapter. Here is the first paragraph.
The practice of interlocking directorates is the root of many evils. It offends laws human and divine. Applied to rival corporations, it tends to the suppression of competition and to violation of the Sherman law. Applied to corporations which deal with each other, it tends to disloyalty and to violation of the fundamental law' that no man can serve two masters. In either event it tends to inefficiency; for it removes incentive and destroys soundness of judgment. It is undemocratic, for it rejects the platform: "A fair field and no favours,"-substituting the pull of privilege for the push of manhood. It is the most potent instrument of the Money Trust. Break the control so exercised by the investment banker over railroads, public service and industrial corporations over banks,
Bank Act

life insurance and trust companies, and a long step will have been taken towards the attainment of the new freedom.
I refer now to a rather humorous specimen prospectus cited by Judge Brandeis on pages 106 and 107.
Has he chapters on the Merchants Bank failure and on the Canadian Bank Act in that book?
No.
If he has not, I submit that my hon. friend should cease leading it.
I submit that the material I have in hand is entirely relevant to the issue under consideration.
Quite the contrary.

I am very glad that I shall

If the hon. member cannot
see the joke I am afraid I am unable to point it out to him. Now, there is a chapter that deals with big men and little business.
I think it is little men talking about big business.

This chapter is particularly
pertinent to the situation in Canada, because there is an inevitable tendency on the part of a number of businesses of various kinds to become concentrated in the hands of a few men. The result is a growth of serious inefficiency in the operation of these businesses.

Is that the case with
the Bank of Montreal?
Or the Farmers Bank?

At page 151 there appears
the following quotation from ex-President Wilson:
I am not saying that all invention had been stQpped by the growth of trusts, but I think it is perfectly clear that invention in many fields has been discouraged, that inventors have been prevented from reaping the full fruits of their ingenuity and industry, and that mankind has been deprived of many comforts and conveniences, as well as the opportunity of buying at lower prices.
Then Mr. Brandeis continues:
The fact that industrial monopolies arrest development is more serious even than the direct burden imposed through extortionate prices. But the most harmbearing incident of the trusts is their promotion of financial concentration. Industrial trusts feed the money trust, practically every trust created has destroyed the financial independence of some communities and of many properties; for it has centred the financing of a large part of whole lines of business in New York, and this usually with one of a few banking houses. This is well illustrated by the Steel Trust, which is a trust of trusts.
He goes on at considerable length to show how the steel trust was formed.
Read chapter 6, verse 4, on co-operative stores.
I shall be glad to read it if the hon. member wants me to.
Yes, I am asking you to read it. Read chapter 6, verse 4.
The hon. member evidently is not acquainted with the book. Chapter 10 is the one that deals with co-operation.
Well, I made a slight mistake.

The first two lines in the chapter read:
We must break the money trust or the money trust will break us.
That is perhaps enough on that point.
That has nothing to do with co-operative stores.

I have in my hand a type written document sent to a fellow-member

Bank Act
by a man who, I understand, lives in western Canada. This document is entitled "Canada -a Dictatorship," and in it there is an examination of the system of interlocking directorates and the concentrtaion of control of Canadian credit, industry, and so forth. I do not wish to quote from it because I have not yet had an opportunity of verifying the statements it contains, but reading it over I can see that the writer has evidently looked into the matter rather carefully. I might mention some of the headings. There are references to "The Power of the Bankers," "The Canadian Cabinet," "The Bank of Montreal," "The Grip Upon Industry," "Financial Corporations," "Fourteen Autocrats," and "A New Phase of Capitalism." I wanted to refer to this document to show that there are some Canadians who are seriously exercised over the situation in Canada, of which, I think, the absorption of the Merchants Bank by the Bank of Montreal is a typical case I mentioned the fact that Judge Brandeis gave a great deal of consideration to the matter on the other side, as have also a great many other prominent Americans. The same drift of affairs is evident on this side of the line as has been evident in the United States, and I would respectfully suggest to the House the great importance of this question and would like to impress upon hon. members the seriousness of the menace that Threatens us to-day in the concentration of control in the hands of a very few men. It is not that the few who form the interlocking directorates of a number of large enterprises actually own those concerns, but 9 p.m. they are so placed that they exercise effective control. It is pointed out in this document that one.group of men in Canada pretty well control assets to the extent of about three and a half billions of dollars. I think, therefore, that I am justified in endeavouring to impress upon the House the very serious nature of the situation and the need of investigating to the very bottom this recent collapse and amalgamation so that we may know what the facts are. Probably we do not know what the extent of the danger is; nor can we know until we have ascertained the facts. Ugly rumours are afloat, and I do think that we should sift the thing to the bottom. As pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary West (M'\ Shaw), there are two purposes in view. The first is to be able intelligently to revise the Bank Act, particularly with respect to those sections that deal with inspection and returns; and the second is to find out whether or not there have been intrigue and shady transactions in connection with this affair, as has been rumoured. I trust that the amendment will secure the support of the House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I desire in a few words to state my reasons for the vote I shall give. I do not want to be understood as voting against any investigation into the Merchants Bank or any other episode; I always feel that if, in cases of alleged wrongdoing, the public is affected, then when a member assumes the proper responsibility for such an allegation, no investigation should be denied. And also there might be a case for investigation, were any wrongdoing alleged, if it were essential for the purposes of intelligent legislation. So the question really is: Is an investigation into this episode necessary to enable us intelligently to legislate as to the Bank Act? I have waited for argument to convince me that it is. One must consider what the public interest is in the Merchants Bank affair.
I do not quite agree with the Minister of Finance that we have no interest merely because-if it were the case-the shareholders alone were affected; it seems to me it is the duty of parliament to guard the interests of shareholders in banking legislation. But we would have an interest much wider and more direct if the depositors were so imperilled, if not actually affected by such actions as we might by legislation prevent the repetition of. Or if holders of bank notes were affected, then our interest would be still more general, more direct and more important. Now, is there reason to believe that there is something connected with the episode still undisclosed that would enable us in this act to protect better the interests of shareholders, or of depositors, or of the holders of bank notes? And there could be one more interest-the general interest of the public who do not want to see a repetition of events that end in the elimination of another bank. I know that in western Canada the case of the Merchants Bank was very widely discussed, as was the case of the Farmers Bank, and I believe the people of that country want to see every precaution taken against the recurrence of such things as result in the elimination of a bank as a separate institution.
Let me inquire again: Has it been shown, has it even been intimated, that there is anything we do not know in connection with the episode that would help us to protect the shareholders, the depositors, the note holders, or help us to prevent the repetition of the incident? If any hon. member had brought
Bank Act

jJ
out a tittle of evidence in support of that, there would be something substantial to discuss. The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) did read from the evidence of Sir John Aird and intimated he had read before I came in from the evidence of Sir Edmund Walker, to the effect that there were some things unknown in connection with the occurrence that led to the merger. Well, I fancy what they must have had reference to was this: They felt, and I believe the bank they were connected with felt, that up to the time of the consent to the merger there had not been disclosure to other banks that might have been just as much interested as the Bank of Montreal, of the exact situation, respecting the Merchants Bank, in order to enable those others to discuss what had taken or was to take place. I think it was felt that there had been too much confinement of the information to one single institution. It may be they had in mind that some facts were still undisclosed that they had a right to know the same as any other bank. I do not know whether they did or not; what those facts could be I do not for the life of me know.
I suggest that that is exactly what we want to find out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Well, shall we postpone revision of the Bank Act simply because some witness suggests that there is something he does not know? What is it? I agree with the Minister of Finance that there were some things connected with the disaster to the Merchants Bank which would help us in the framing of this act. But were these not all brought out in the trial? What are we interested in? We are interested to see that every precaution is taken to prevent the nondisclosure to the government of Canada of vital information, of essential information connected with the management. Everything associated with that came out in the trial of these men. I wonder how many hon. gentlemen in this House have read the evidenca taken at the trial? I cannot boast of having done so myself-that is to say, in the original though I have done so very carefully from more than one newspaper that reported the evidence pretty fully. So far as I could see, everything connected with that subject came out in the trial and it should have been known to the committee when the committee sat What perhaps did not come out was an answer to the question -why these loans were made. Well, how in the world can this House ever legislate to prevent the making of bad loans' Hon. gentlemen say that $10,000,000 went 
through a hole. I suppose it did; but I can name more than one company right now through a hole in whose organization more than $10,000,000 has gone. I venture to say it would not be hard to name other banks and to point to an end of this country that might be called a hole through which $10,000,000 of the money of these banks has gone. How this can be prevented unless by making men wiser than they are I do not know. Now, everything that we are interested in is to know what precautions can be taken by parliament. All that parliament can do is to get the best information, to get all the information, required from time to time. We know that now; what other information can we ask for that is not asked for in the act? If there is any other, let us put it in. I understand that amendments have been made to the act as a result of the evidence at the trials and of the findings of the committee. Perhaps they would have been in anyway, 1 do not know; but I am informed that they are the result of the findings. One of them, for example, is the double audit system; another, a better definition of the responsibility of directors; another, the protection of the employees' insurance fund.
And another, contact between the shareholders' auditors and the directors.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Very well; I was not
aware of that. The facts that affected the government, that affected the public, that affected parliament, were disclosed in these hearings. The facts that are undisclosed- if there are any, I do not know what they are-are connected with the making of a loan to a brokerage firm in Montreal that evidently should not have been made. But you may frame acts of parliament until parliament is grey and you cannot prevent bank managements from making loans that are bad. Consequently, I do not see why We should defer the passing of the Bank Act in order that there may be further investigation into this failure, or into this episode, however you may describe it. As soon as anyone can show me that by the holding of an investigation there is something to be gained in the way of light upon the Bank Act itself or how to frame it, then, whether wrong-doing is alleged or not, I will not vote against the investigation. But merely because someone says, "Well, if we fished along a bit there might be something," then I feel I would be giving a reckless, an arbitrary, an unreasoned vote in supporting delay for a year on that account.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to
refer on this motion to two matters. The first is to recall a question which I put to the government last Friday, and in which I called attention to the inability of certain of the active militia to vote in the approaching provincial election in Ontario and asked that arrangements be made in such a way that those members would not be disfranchised. The Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) went into the matter as he had promised, and in conversation with officers of the department, ascertained that the date had been fixed three or four months ago and two or three months before the date of the Ontario elections was announced; furthermore that as, under present estimates, only eight days' training is allowed, anything

in the nature of a three-day break in the middle would, of course, destroy the effect of the entire training and, as was urged and as, I believe, was right, was out of the question. A deferring would have meant a cost of many thousands of dollars. The Acting Minister of National Defence reported those circumstances to the House; he stated that he was sending to the Attorney General of Ontario a telegram setting out the facts I have recited and requesting that the attorney general instruct the returning officers affected in about five cities to admit these votes at the advance polls, and he undertook if legislation were necessary to ratify, to support such legislation in the next House if he were still in the government. Detachments of batteries from Gananoque, Belleville, Peterborough, Guelph, Hamilton, Cobourg, schedule to train at Petawawa overlapping polling date June 25. Alternative is for you to permit votes to be cast in home towns prior to departure under terms of advance polling provision your election act. If legislation does not give power suggest that above action be taken and ratified at next session of your legislature. Am informed Mr. Ferguson who is now here will agree to this' proposal. Premier King approves of this proposal. If you agree public announcement should be made at once. Reply.
On the 16th, the following reply was received, not from Mr. Raney, but from Mr. A. M. Dymond, the chief election officer of the province:
Your wire addressed to attorney general referred to me, no authority whatever for action suggested by you. Would advise postponement of entrainment for camp until after polling day, announcement made more than month ago of date of pollings.

Elections and Petawawa Camp
In answer to this the following telegram was sent tc the lion. Mr. Raney himself. It was not addressed to Mr. Dymond, because we felt that the attorney general of the province ought to deal with an important matter of this kind himself. On the 18th of June we addressed this telegram to the Hon. Mr. Raney:
Following wire received:
Here we quoted in full telegram received from Mr. Dymond.
Dates of training Petawawa fixed over three months ago. Detachments from Ontario, Quebec and Maritime provinces involved. In view of heavy expense entailed and interference with private arrangements of members non-permanent active militia no alteration dates practicable. Propose publish my wire June 15th.
That was on the 18th of June, and so far there has been no reply. I shall briefly state the situation. Six batteries of artillery consisting of 38 officers and men each, or a total of 2S2 men, entrained on Friday to go to camp at Petawawa, where they will spend eight days, including the day occupied in going out and the day in coming back. Their training is of a special nature which can be given only at Petawawa, and includes three days of shooting in addition to other necessary drill and training in other respects. I may observe that Mr. Hay, the leader of the Liberal party in Ontario, was communicated with on the day on which the telegram was sent to Mr. Raney. The right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) properly states that the only way in which these men can exercise the franchise, if they go into camp at Petawawa, will be for the provincial authorities of Ontario to arrange for the taking of advanced polls. I am informed by the officers of my department that it would involve the country in a loss of between $7,000 or $8,000 if any change were made now in the dates fixed for this training, which dates were settled upon long before any provincial or other election was in prospect. I am surprised that the authorities in Ontario have not responded to our suggestion. I do think that an arrangement might have been made between the different political parties by which the votes of these men might be taken to-morrow or Friday before they entrained for camp. As Petawawa is a little to the west of the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway in the northern part of the province there would be great difficulty, even if it were practicable, for any of the officers or men to get to their homes to vote, for it would take them at least three days to accomplish this purpose. Obviously therefore the only means of having them exercise the franchise is that which we have suggested.

I think the minister
might give us a statement of the present position of this matter, having regard to the attitude of Ontario on the one hand and of Manitoba on the other, as well as that of the Dominion government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS ONTARIO ELECTIONS AND PETAWAWA CAMP
speechtext:
This bill is the same as the one that was introduced last year and accepted by the House of Commons, but rejected by the Senate. The purpose of the bill is to repeal chapter 38. 11 and 12 George V, passed in 1921 and assented to on the 4th of June of that year. In 1920, there was an understanding between the Ontario government and the Dominion government to the effect that a commission composed of four members, two to be appointed by the Ontario government and two by the Dominion government, would t control the waters of the Lake of the Woods, Lac Seul, English river and Winnipeg river. It was agreed that legislation should be submitted to the legislature

Lake of the Woods Regulation
of Ontario and the parliament of Canada for the purpose of organizing that com-
10 p.m. mission. The Dominion government accordingly introduced a bill which passed as chapter 10, of 11 and 12 George V, which was assented to on the 3rd of May, 1921. The government of Ontario, proceeding also in accordance with the agreement to which I have referred, introduced similar legislation; but the premier of the province, facing an opposition to the measure, withdrew it. Under these circumstances the government of the day, considering it important that some commission should have authority to control these waters, passed another bill, which became chapter 38 of 11 and 12 George V, to which I referred at the outset. The second clause of that act provided that-
All dams, structures and other works of whatsoever description which have heretofore been or may hereafter be constructed in, upin, over, about or across,- (a) any outlet of the Lake of the Woods, (b) the Winnipeg river at or about its junction with English river, or (c) English river at the outlet of and below Lac Seul, which do or may or can in any wise control, regulate or affect the outflow of water from the said lakes, or either of them, or the natural levels of the water in the said lakes, or either of them, at any time, or the natural flow of the water in the Winnipeg river or in English river, at any time, are and each of them is declared to be for the general advantage of Canada.
The last clause reads as follows:
If the necessary legislation of Ontario referred to in the preamble of The Lake of the Woods Control Board Act, 1921-
That is, chapter 10.
-be enacted by the legislature, the Governor in Council may, by proclamation published in the Canada Gazette, repeal or suspend this act and the regulations made thereunder at any time when or after The Lake of the Woods Control Board Act, 1921, shall come into force: Provided that notwithstanding any repeal or suspension of this act in the manner provided by this section the works and each of them hereby declared to be for the general advantage of Canada shall remain and continue to be works for the general advantage of Canada.
Acting under the provisions of that statute the government of the day appointed a commission, also composed of four members, as agreed upon. I understand that the government of Ontario was asked to appoint two of the members of the commission but they refused to do so, contending that this statute should never have been passed and that the works of the Lake of the Woods, the English River and the Winnipeg river should not have been declared works for the general advantage of Canada. Last year the then Solicitor General introduced a bill similar to the one now under consideration. I may say that in the session following the Act of 1921 the legislature of Ontario did pass the legis-

lation which had been agreed upon, and last session the then Solicitor General thought we should simply repeal chapter 38 of the statutes of 1921. After some debate the bill was adopted by the House but was subsequently rejected by the Senate. After prorogation, at the instance of the premiers of Ontario and Manitoba, a conference took place in Ottawa in which the premiers of those provinces and the Prime Minister of Canada took part. After discussion and deliberation the representatives of the three governments arrived at an understanding which was put in writing and signed by them. The first clause of that agreement reads as follows:
This agreement, as a working basis for the regulation of the English and Winnipeg rivers, is entered into on the understanding that all parties are agreeable to the repeal of the Lake of the Woods Regulation Act, 1921, but Ontario does not bind itself to the terms of this agreement in the event of that act not being repealed.
Then follow the different clauses which were accepted by the three parties. Consequent upon these circumstances we introduced the present bill. After it was read the first time representations were made to us first by the government of Manitoba and afterwards by the government of Ontario. The government of Manitoba urged that chapter 38 of the Statutes of 1921 should not be repealed until the provisions of the arrangement of November last had been fulfilled. We had a conference and listened to the arguments of the representatives of Manitoba. We told them that this bill would come into force only by proclamation, and that that proclamation should be made only when the essential conditions of the arrangement entered into had been fulfilled. Subsequently the representatives of the Manitoba government wrote a letter to the Prime Minister stating that they could not accept the suggestion that we should proceed with this bill at the present session. In reply the right hon. Prime Minister wrote the following letter to Mr. Farmer, the mayor of Winnipeg:
Dear Mr. Farmer:
I have duly received the letter dated the 29th instant signed by yourself and Messrs. Preudhomme, Sanger, Guy and Johnson, with respect to the above.
You are quite correct in your understanding that the repeal act should not become effective until the conditions of the agreement of November last have been complied with. You suggest that the repeal bill should be amended in such a way as to provide that it shall go into effect on proclamation only after Ontario and Manitoba respectively have so requested by order in council. With reference to this suggestion I would like to point out that the bill has been drafted in a matter which would permit of ho exception being taken by the Ontario government to it.

Lake of the Woods Regulation
provisions. Were the conditions you propose incorporated, it might only serve to raise a fresh obstacle to the final settlement of this whole matter, which is now so near the point of satisfactory adjustment. Our government has in view but the one object of effecting a settlement of the question in a manner which will be wholly satisfactory to all parties concerned. We are as favourably disposed toward the province of Manitoba as toward the province of Ontario, and, inasmuch as the federal government, not less than the governments of Ontario and Manitoba, is a party to the agreement of November last, I think you may take it for granted that we would not take any action or permit any action to be taken which would prejudice the right of either Manitoba or Ontario under any of the conditions of the agreement.
With this assurance I hope you will feel that Manitoba will be justified in withdrawing any opposition it may have to the Repeal Bill in the form in which it has been presented to parliament.
With this assurance, Mr. Speaker, given by the right hon. the Prime Minister of this Dominion speaking for himself and for his colleagues, I do not see that the government of Manitoba can persist in any opposition to the measure.

I have here a letter which was written by the Hon. Mr. Johnson, counsel for Manitoba and the power interests, dated June 18th, which reads as follows:
On the 31st ultimo you wrote a letter to Mayor S. J. Farmer of Winnipeg on this subject, and you very kindly sent me a copy thereof. We note that you desire to take no step which would permit of any exception being taken by the Ontario government to the repealing of the above act. We would, however, point out that the order in council passed by the province of Ontario in connection with the agreement entered into last November makes the absolute repeal of "The Lake of the Woods Regulation Act, 1921," a condition precedent to the coming into force of the agreement, and also to the empowering of the minister mentioned therein to finally negotiate and settle upon the conditions to be carried out; this attitude of Ontario will make impossible the carrying out of the conditions of the agreement prior to the proclamation of the repealing act.
